<!-- Source: README.md -->

# @codenhub/i18n

Translate your app's text with typed keys, ICU messages, plurals, and fallback languages, in the browser, on a server, or at build time.

## Installation

```sh
pnpm add @codenhub/i18n
```

## Usage

```ts
// src/i18n.ts
import { createI18n } from "@codenhub/i18n";

const dictionaries = {
  en: { home: { title: "Welcome", greeting: "Hello, {name}!" }, cart: { items: { one: "{count} item", other: "{count} items" } } },
  pt: { home: { title: "Bem-vindo", greeting: "Olá, {name}!" }, cart: { items: { one: "{count} item", other: "{count} itens" } } },
} as const;

export const i18n = createI18n({
  locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  loadLocale: (locale) => dictionaries[locale],
});

export const { t } = i18n;
```

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { i18n, t } from "./i18n";

await i18n.init({ locale: "pt" });

t("home.greeting", { name: "Ana" }); // "Olá, Ana!"
t("cart.items", { count: 3 }); // "3 itens"
t("home.titel"); // compile error: there is no such key
```

That last line is the point of the whole package: the typo fails in your editor, not in front of a Portuguese visitor. Await `init()` before calling `t()`, which throws until the manager has started.

Two optional entry points cover what differs by environment:

- `@codenhub/i18n/browser` detects the visitor's language, remembers the one your app chooses, keeps `<html lang>` and `dir` in step, and can translate HTML marked with `data-i18n`.
- `@codenhub/i18n/routing` reads and builds localized paths, such as `/pt/about` or `/pt/sobre`, and can drop the locale prefix where a path is unambiguous, as in `/sobre`.

## Documentation

- [Overview](docs/index.md): the ideas behind the package and a walkthrough.
- [Write your translations](docs/translations.md): JSON files, ICU messages, plurals, regional variants, and typed keys and values.
- [Translate a browser app](docs/browser.md), including in a Web Worker.
- [Render on a server or at build time](docs/server-rendering.md)
- [Localized URLs](docs/localized-urls.md)
- [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md)
- [API reference](docs/reference/index.md)
- [Changelog](docs/changelog/index.md)

## Requirements

- An ESM-aware bundler or runtime.
- Node.js 24 or newer, or a current Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit browser or Web Worker.
- No runtime dependencies.

In a Web Worker, the root entry point and `@codenhub/i18n/routing` work as anywhere else. `@codenhub/i18n/browser` works only with `syncDocument: false` and no `root`, since a worker has no page; with the defaults it throws a `TypeError` before starting the manager. See [In a Web Worker](docs/browser.md#in-a-web-worker).

## Notes

- On a server or in a static build, create one manager per request or page, not a shared one. A shared manager is how one visitor ends up reading another visitor's language.
- The package does not render HTML from translations: text always comes back as text.
- ICU messages cover `number`, `date`, `time`, `plural`, `selectordinal`, and `select`, without number skeletons or styles such as `{n, number, currency}`, which are shown as written with a warning. Format such a value with `formatNumber()` and pass the result in.

# Translate your app

`@codenhub/i18n` turns keys such as `"home.title"` into text in the reader's language. You write your translations as plain objects or JSON files, one per language, and the package does the rest: it loads the right one, falls back to your main language when a translation is missing, fills in values like names and counts, writes numbers and dates the way the reader expects, and tells TypeScript which keys exist, so a typo fails to compile instead of reaching production.

The core works the same in a browser, a Node.js server, a static site build, or a Web Worker. Two optional extras handle the jobs that differ by environment:

- **`@codenhub/i18n/browser`** picks the visitor's language, remembers their choice, keeps the page's `lang` and `dir` attributes in step, and can translate HTML marked with `data-i18n`. Most of that needs a page, so in a Web Worker, which has none, it takes two extra options; see [In a Web Worker](docs/browser.md#in-a-web-worker).
- **`@codenhub/i18n/routing`** puts the language in the URL, as in `/pt/about`, and can translate the path itself, as in `/pt/sobre` or `/sobre`. It only reads and builds strings, so it works anywhere, a Worker included.

## Four ideas

The whole package fits in four ideas. No fifth one is hiding in a footnote.

**A locale** names a language, and sometimes a region: `en`, `pt`, `pt-BR`, `ar`. You list the locales your app supports, and pick one as the **default locale**: the language your app is written in first, which every other locale falls back to.

**A dictionary** holds every translation for one locale. Keys can be nested to keep related text together:

```json
{
  "home": {
    "title": "Welcome",
    "greeting": "Hello, {name}!"
  }
}
```

Nested keys are joined with dots, so this dictionary has the keys `home.title` and `home.greeting`.

**A loader** is a function you write that returns the dictionary for a locale. It can return an object you imported, read a file, or fetch JSON from your server. The package never decides where translations live; it calls your loader when it needs a locale, and keeps the result.

**A manager** ties these together. You create one with `createI18n()`, tell it which locale to use, and ask it for text with `t()`.

## Walkthrough

### 1. Install

```sh
pnpm add @codenhub/i18n
```

The package is an ES module and needs Node.js 24 or newer, or a current browser. It has no runtime dependencies.

### 2. Write two dictionaries

Start with your default language and one more. Here they are objects in a TypeScript file; [Write your translations](docs/translations.md) shows how to keep them in JSON files instead.

```ts
// src/locales.ts
export const dictionaries = {
  en: {
    home: { title: "Welcome", greeting: "Hello, {name}!" },
    cart: { items: { one: "{count} item", other: "{count} items" } },
  },
  pt: {
    home: { title: "Bem-vindo", greeting: "Olá, {name}!" },
    cart: { items: { one: "{count} item", other: "{count} itens" } },
  },
} as const;
```

The `as const` lets TypeScript see the exact keys, so it can check every `t()` call against them.

### 3. Create the manager

In a browser app, create the manager once in its own module and import it wherever you need text:

```ts
// src/i18n.ts
import { createI18n } from "@codenhub/i18n";
import { dictionaries } from "./locales";

export const i18n = createI18n({
  locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  loadLocale: (locale) => dictionaries[locale],
});

export const { t } = i18n;
```

`t` is a short name for `i18n.translate`. Every method on the manager works on its own after you pull it off, like `t` here, so you can import `t` directly.

On a server, one shared manager is the wrong shape; [Render on a server](docs/server-rendering.md#one-manager-per-request) explains why, and what to do instead.

### 4. Start it, then translate

The manager has to load a dictionary before it can translate, so start it once when your app starts and wait for it:

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { i18n, t } from "./i18n";

await i18n.init({ locale: "pt" });

t("home.title"); // "Bem-vindo"
t("home.greeting", { name: "Ana" }); // "Olá, Ana!"
t("cart.items", { count: 3 }); // "3 itens"
t("home.titel"); // compile error: there is no such key
```

`init()` without a locale starts with the default locale. Calling `t()` before `init()` has finished throws an error, because there is nothing to translate with yet.

### 5. Switch languages

```ts
await i18n.setLocale("en");
t("home.title"); // "Welcome"
```

`setLocale()` loads the new dictionary first and only switches once it has loaded, so text never shows half in one language and half in another. To redraw your interface when the language changes, pass a function to `i18n.subscribe()`. It runs after every `init()` and every language switch that actually happens; [Keep track of the manager](#keep-track-of-the-manager) says exactly when that is.

## What happens when a translation is missing

Translations rarely stay complete. A feature ships in English on Tuesday and in Portuguese whenever the translator gets to it. The package handles the gap in two steps:

1. **The key is missing in the current locale but present in the default one**, or in a parent locale, such as `pt` for `pt-BR` (see [Regional variants](docs/translations.md#regional-variants)). You get that text. In the example above, a key only in `en` shows English to Portuguese readers. Nothing is logged, because this is normal while translators catch up; [a key check in your tests](docs/translations.md#find-untranslated-keys) finds these.
2. **The key is missing everywhere.** `t()` returns the key, trimmed, such as `"home.subtitle"`, so the gap is visible on screen and easy to search for.

In the second case, the manager also logs a warning, such as `[I18n] Missing key "home.subtitle" in locale "pt".`. It warns once for each locale and key pair, so a key used on every render doesn't flood the console. It remembers the 1,000 most recent pairs, so a pair that drops off that list can warn again. A manager created with `isSilent: true` never logs it. To send misses to your own logger instead, pass `onMissingKey(key, locale)`: it replaces the warning and runs on every miss, not once per pair.

`t()` always returns a string, so you never need `?? ""` after it.

## Right-to-left languages

Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, and Urdu are written right to left. A page in one of them must say so with `<html dir="rtl">`, or the browser aligns the text to the wrong side and puts punctuation at the wrong end of the sentence. The manager knows the direction of its active locale as `i18n.direction`, which is `"ltr"` or `"rtl"`:

```ts
await i18n.init({ locale: "ar" });
i18n.direction; // "rtl"
```

The browser binding writes it to `<html dir>` for you. On a server, write it into the page yourself, as in [Render on a server](docs/server-rendering.md#one-manager-per-request).

### How the default decides

A locale is `rtl` when the script it is written in runs right to left. The script is the locale's script subtag when it has one, such as `Arab` in `uz-Arab`. Otherwise it is the script the language is most likely written in, which `Intl.Locale`'s `maximize()` works out from the language and the region:

| Locale                 | Direction | Why                                                           |
| ---------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ar`, `he`, `fa`, `ur` | `rtl`     | Arabic and Hebrew scripts.                                    |
| `uz-Arab`              | `rtl`     | The script subtag says Arabic.                                |
| `pa`                   | `ltr`     | Punjabi is most likely written in Gurmukhi.                   |
| `pa-PK`                | `rtl`     | In Pakistan, Punjabi is most likely written in Arabic script. |
| `sd-IN`                | `ltr`     | In India, Sindhi is most likely written in Devanagari.        |
| `en`, `pt-BR`          | `ltr`     | Latin script.                                                 |

The region is why a plain list of languages would get this wrong: `pa` and `pa-PK` are the same language in two scripts. For a tag `Intl.Locale` can't read, a fixed list of right-to-left languages, such as `ar` and `he`, decides instead.

The likely-script data comes with the JavaScript engine, and for rare tags it can differ between engine versions. When a tag is ambiguous, the tag is usually the better fix: `sd-Arab-IN` says Arabic script outright, and the default reads it as `rtl`.

### Set the direction yourself

Pass `getLocaleDirection` to decide for every locale. It replaces the default entirely, so it must answer for all of them:

```ts
export const i18n = createI18n({
  locales: ["en", "ar"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  loadLocale: (locale) => dictionaries[locale],
  getLocaleDirection: (locale) => (locale === "ar" ? "rtl" : "ltr"),
});
```

The manager calls it for the default locale when it is created, and for each locale it starts or switches to. Two ways it can fail:

- **It returns something other than `"ltr"` or `"rtl"`.** That throws `TypeError: [I18n] Invalid direction for locale "ar".`: from `createI18n()` when the answer for the default locale is wrong, or from the `init()` or `setLocale()` that asked, which leaves the manager in its current language. Return exactly one of the two strings.
- **It throws.** Your error is not wrapped or swallowed: it comes out of `createI18n()`, `init()`, or `setLocale()` unchanged, and a failed switch again leaves the current language in place.

## Keep track of the manager

The manager has a few properties you can read at any time:

- `i18n.locale` is the active locale. Before `init()` has finished, it is the default locale.
- `i18n.isReady` is `false` until the first `init()` succeeds, then `true`. While it is `false`, `t()` throws.
- `i18n.direction` is the active locale's direction, as above.
- `i18n.locales`, `i18n.defaultLocale`, and `i18n.isSilent` are what you configured. `locales` is a frozen copy.

### React to changes

`subscribe(listener)` calls `listener`, without arguments, after every applied `init()` and every applied locale change, and returns a function that stops it. "Applied" is doing real work in that sentence: a `setLocale()` to the locale already active changes nothing, and neither does a call that a later one overtook (next section), so neither calls the listener. Calling `init()` again with the same locale does apply, and does call it.

For code that needs to know what changed, the manager is also an `EventTarget` with two events:

- `ready`, after every applied `init()`. `event.detail.locale` is the locale it started with.
- `locale-change`, after every applied locale change. `event.detail.locale` is the new locale and `event.detail.previousLocale` the one before it.

```ts
i18n.addEventListener("locale-change", (event) => {
  console.info(`Language changed from ${event.detail.previousLocale} to ${event.detail.locale}`);
});
```

Listeners run in the order they were added. An exception in a listener or a `subscribe()` function is reported as for any `EventTarget`: in a browser, as an uncaught error that neither stops the other listeners nor undoes the change; in Node.js, it crashes the process, which [Render on a server](docs/server-rendering.md#keep-production-logs-useful) comes back to.

### The latest call wins

Loading takes time, and people click faster than networks answer. When `init()` or `setLocale()` calls overlap, the one started last decides the language. An earlier call that finishes loading after a later one has started resolves without applying anything: no locale change, no event, no `subscribe()` call.

Say a visitor reading in Spanish clicks "Português" in your language picker, then "English" before Portuguese has loaded:

```ts
const portuguese = i18n.setLocale("pt"); // first click
const english = i18n.setLocale("en"); // second click
await Promise.all([portuguese, english]);
i18n.locale; // "en": the Portuguese call resolved, but changed nothing
```

So after `await i18n.setLocale("pt")`, don't assume the locale is `pt`; read `i18n.locale` when the outcome matters. A later `setLocale()` to the locale already active counts as a later call too: it cancels a pending switch, and the visitor stays where they are. A call that fails rejects and leaves the current language as it was.

### Turn outside input into a locale

`init()` and `setLocale()` throw a `RangeError` for a locale that isn't in `locales`. A locale from a cookie, a query string, or a request header is untrusted text, so turn it into a configured locale first. Two methods do that, for two kinds of input.

**`resolveLocale(value)`** is for a value that should already be one of your locales, such as a `?lang=` parameter or a cookie your app wrote. It accepts exact matches only, ignoring letter case and surrounding spaces, and returns your spelling of the locale, or `undefined`:

```ts
const lang = new URL(location.href).searchParams.get("lang") ?? "";
await i18n.init({ locale: i18n.resolveLocale(lang) ?? i18n.defaultLocale });
// ?lang=PT-br starts in "pt-BR"; ?lang=fr, or no lang, starts in the default.
```

**`matchLocale(preferences)`** is for a visitor's language preferences, such as `navigator.languages` or the languages of an `Accept-Language` header, most preferred first. It finds the closest locale you support. Each preference is tried in order, and the first one that matches anything wins:

1. An exact match, ignoring case: `pt-BR` gets `pt-BR`.
2. The longest configured locale the preference starts with, as whole subtags, written in the same script: `pt-BR` gets `pt`.
3. A match through likely subtags: `zh-TW`, Traditional Chinese, gets `zh-Hant`.
4. The same language in the same script: `pt-PT` gets `pt-BR` when that is your only Portuguese.

Norwegian has two codes for Bokmål, `no` and `nb`, and browsers send either, so they count as one language: a site configured with `no` serves a visitor who sends `nb`, and the other way round. Nynorsk, `nn`, is its own written standard and never matches them.

A locale in another script never matches, because a page in a script the visitor doesn't read serves them worse than their next language. With `zh`, which is Simplified Chinese, a `zh-TW` visitor who also lists English gets English, and one who lists nothing else gets `undefined`. A configured locale that `Intl.Locale` rejects, such as one with a private-use subtag over eight characters, has no likely script, so it matches by language, and by the script it names when it names one.

It returns `undefined` when nothing matches, skips blank and malformed entries, and throws a `TypeError` when `preferences` isn't an array.

When several of your locales share a language and script, and none matches a preference exactly or by its likely region, the first one in `locales` wins. So order `locales` by which one should serve everyone else. To serve a visitor from Mexico, `es-MX`, from your Latin American Spanish, list `es-419` before `es-ES`:

```ts
const i18n = createI18n({
  locales: ["en", "es-419", "es-ES"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  loadLocale: (locale) => dictionaries[locale],
});

i18n.matchLocale(["es-MX"]); // "es-419", because it is listed first
i18n.matchLocale(["es"]); // "es-ES", since Spanish without a region most likely means Spain
```

## What this package does not do

It translates, formats, and picks locales. A few things are deliberately left out:

- **HTML in translations.** `t()` returns plain text, and `data-i18n` sets plain text, so `"<strong>Hi</strong>"` shows its tags rather than bold text. Keep markup in your templates or components, and put only words in the dictionary, with [placeholders](docs/translations.md#put-values-into-text) for values.
- **Number skeletons and currency in messages.** ICU skeletons such as `{price, number, ::currency/EUR}`, and the `currency` style, `{price, number, currency}`, are not supported: a message can't know which currency a price is in. Format the amount in code with `i18n.formatNumber(9.99, { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" })` and pass the string. A message that uses one is invalid syntax and shows as written; see [Format numbers and dates in the text](docs/translations.md#format-numbers-and-dates-in-the-text) for what is supported.
- **Loading translations.** The package calls your loader; where the files live, how they are fetched, cached, or retried, is yours.
- **Routes, redirects, and navigation.** Locale routing reads and builds paths, but your framework or server still registers routes, redirects, and navigates.

## Where to go next

Read these in order to learn the package end to end, or jump to the one you need:

1. [Write your translations](docs/translations.md): dictionaries, JSON files, placeholders, ICU messages, plurals, formatters, typed keys and values, checking for untranslated keys, and size limits.
2. [Translate a browser app](docs/browser.md): detect and remember the visitor's language, keep `lang` and `dir` in step, re-render a framework, and translate HTML with `data-i18n`.
3. [Render on a server or at build time](docs/server-rendering.md): one manager per request, choosing a locale from `Accept-Language`, time zones, quiet logs, and static site builds.
4. [Localized URLs](docs/localized-urls.md): put the locale in the path, translate the path itself, link to other languages, generate every localized page, and detect the language on a static site.
5. [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md): what each error and warning means, and how to fix it.

Two more pages are for looking things up rather than reading through: the [API reference](docs/reference/index.md) lists every export, option, and type, and the [changelog](docs/changelog/index.md) says what changed in each version and how to upgrade.

<!-- Source: docs/translations.md -->

# Write your translations

A dictionary is a plain object whose values are strings or more objects. This page covers how to organize dictionaries, load them, put values and counts into text, keep TypeScript checking all of it, and keep every language complete. It builds on the `en` and `pt` dictionaries from the [overview](docs/index.md#walkthrough).

## Dictionary shape

Nest keys to group related text. Every leaf must be a string:

```json
{
  "nav": { "home": "Home", "settings": "Settings" },
  "settings": {
    "title": "Settings",
    "language": { "label": "Language", "hint": "Used across the whole app" }
  }
}
```

The manager flattens nesting into dot-separated keys: `nav.home`, `settings.language.hint`. You can also write flat keys directly, as `{ "nav.home": "Home" }`, or mix both, as long as two spellings never produce the same key.

A dictionary is rejected with a `TypeError` when it contains something that is not text or a group, such as a number, an array, or `null`, or a key the manager can't use, such as `"nav..home"` or `" home"` with a leading space. The error names the locale and the key, as in `[I18n] Invalid locale dictionary key "nav. home" in locale "pt".`; [A dictionary is rejected](docs/troubleshooting.md#a-dictionary-is-rejected) goes through every rule and its fix.

An empty dictionary is fine. A locale you have added but not translated yet starts normally and shows default-locale text everywhere.

## Keep dictionaries in JSON files

Most apps keep one JSON file per locale, often because translators or a translation service edit them:

```text
src/locales/
  en.json
  pt.json
```

Load them with a dynamic `import()`, so a visitor downloads only the languages the manager needs: their own, plus your default language as the fallback:

```ts
import { createI18n } from "@codenhub/i18n";
import type en from "./locales/en.json";

export const i18n = createI18n({
  locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  async loadLocale(locale): Promise<typeof en> {
    const module = await import(`./locales/${locale}.json`);
    return module.default;
  },
});
```

This shares one manager across a browser app. On a server or in a static build, wrap `createI18n()` in a function and call it for each request or page instead, as [Render on a server](docs/server-rendering.md#one-manager-per-request) explains.

The return type `Promise<typeof en>` is what gives you typed keys: a dynamic import returns `any`, which would otherwise let any string through. `import type` needs `"resolveJsonModule": true` in your `tsconfig.json`, and never ends up in your bundle.

To fetch dictionaries from a server instead, return the parsed JSON, throw on a failed response, and give up after a while:

```ts
async loadLocale(locale): Promise<typeof en> {
  const response = await fetch(`/locales/${locale}.json`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Locale request failed: ${response.status}`);
  return response.json();
}
```

The `throw` makes the manager report the failure instead of loading your 404 page as a dictionary. The timeout matters more than it looks; the next section says why.

Your loader owns everything about transport: URLs, caching headers, retries, timeouts, and credentials. The manager only calls it and checks what comes back.

### How loading behaves

- The manager loads a locale the first time it needs it and keeps the result, so switching back to a language does not call your loader again.
- Starting or switching to a non-default locale loads that locale, the locales it falls back to, and the default locale together, as [Regional variants](#regional-variants) explains.
- If your loader throws or rejects, the call that needed it rejects with an `I18nError`, and the manager keeps its current language. The next call tries the loader again. [Loading a locale fails](docs/troubleshooting.md#loading-a-locale-fails-with-i18nerror) shows how to show that error to the visitor.
- While a locale is loading, every other call that needs it waits on the same load rather than calling your loader again. So a loader that never settles, such as a `fetch()` to a server that accepts the connection and then says nothing, blocks that locale for good: every later `setLocale()` to it, a retry button included, waits on the same stuck promise. Make your loader time out, as with `AbortSignal.timeout()` above; a timeout rejects, and the next call tries again.
- Returning the same object every time, such as a module-level import, lets every manager share one checked copy. That matters on a server, which [creates a manager per request](docs/server-rendering.md).
- Treat a dictionary as read-only once loaded: the manager keeps a frozen, checked copy, shared by every manager that loads the same object, so later changes to the object do nothing.

## Regional variants

A regional locale only needs the words that differ. With `pt` and `pt-BR` both in `locales`, `pt-BR.json` can hold just the Brazilian words, and every other key comes from `pt.json`:

```ts
export const i18n = createI18n({
  locales: ["en", "pt", "pt-BR"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  loadLocale: (locale) => dictionaries[locale],
});
// pt-BR: { "greeting": "Oi" }   pt: { "greeting": "Olá", "farewell": "Tchau" }
await i18n.init({ locale: "pt-BR" });
t("greeting"); // "Oi"
t("farewell"); // "Tchau", from pt
```

A key is looked up in the active locale, then in each configured locale made by dropping its last subtags, such as `zh-Hant` for `zh-Hant-TW`, then in the default locale. A parent written in another script is skipped: `zh` is Simplified Chinese, so a `zh-Hant` page falls back to the default rather than mixing scripts. A plural group uses the rules of the locale whose dictionary has it.

Every locale in that chain loads with the active one, so starting in `pt-BR` loads `pt-BR`, `pt`, and `en`. If one of them fails, the call rejects as for any locale.

Only parents made by dropping subtags count. `es-MX` does not fall back to `es-419`, because `es-419` is not a shorter version of it; give it its own dictionary, or serve Mexican visitors from `es-419` directly, as [Turn outside input into a locale](docs/index.md#turn-outside-input-into-a-locale) shows.

## Put values into text

Write `{name}` where a value goes, and pass the value to `t()`:

```json
{ "welcome": "Welcome back, {name}. You have {count} new messages." }
```

```ts
t("welcome", { name: "Ana", count: 4 });
// "Welcome back, Ana. You have 4 new messages."
```

Values can be strings, numbers, or dates. Placeholder names use ASCII letters, digits, and `_`, such as `{firstName}` or `{first_name}`. A name with anything else, such as `{first-name}` or `{nome_ç}`, is not a placeholder: the message is invalid syntax, logs a warning, and shows `{first-name}` as written.

Use placeholders instead of joining fragments. `t("before") + name + t("after")` locks every language into English word order, while a whole sentence with a placeholder lets each translation put the value where it belongs.

A few details:

- A placeholder with no matching value stays as written, so a missing value shows up as `{name}` on screen rather than disappearing.
- Numbers in a plain `{name}` are inserted as JavaScript writes them: `1234.5`. Write `{name, number}` to format them for the reader, as the next section shows.
- Braces and apostrophes are message syntax, so text that shows them literally needs quoting; see [Literal braces and apostrophes](#literal-braces-and-apostrophes).

### Format numbers and dates in the text

Messages use [ICU MessageFormat](https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/format_parse/messages/) syntax, so a translation can say how each value is written:

```json
{
  "total": "Total: {amount, number}",
  "progress": "{ratio, number, percent} done",
  "shipped": "Shipped on {date, date, long} at {date, time, short}"
}
```

```ts
t("total", { amount: 1234.5 }); // "Total: 1,234.5", or "Total: 1.234,5" from the Portuguese text
t("shipped", { date: new Date() });
```

| Argument                | Styles                                                             | Value                 |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------- |
| `{n, number}`           | none, `integer`, `percent`                                         | number                |
| `{d, date}`             | `short`, `medium` (the default), `long`, `full`                    | `Date` or a timestamp |
| `{d, time}`             | `short`, `medium` (the default), `long`, `full`                    | `Date` or a timestamp |
| `{n, plural, …}`        | see [Plurals](#plurals)                                            | number                |
| `{n, selectordinal, …}` | ordinal forms, such as `one {#st} two {#nd} few {#rd} other {#th}` | number                |
| `{v, select, …}`        | any words, plus `other`                                            | string or number      |

Formatting uses the language of the dictionary the text came from, so English text that fills in for a missing Portuguese key is written the English way. An argument whose value has the wrong type, such as a string for `{n, number}`, stays as written.

Two things messages can't do, both on purpose:

- **Skeletons and currency.** `{n, number, ::currency/EUR}` and `{n, number, currency}` are invalid syntax: a translation can't know which currency the amount is in. Format the amount in code, as below, and pass the string.
- **Nesting past 10 levels.** A `plural` or `select` can sit inside another one's options, up to 10 levels deep. An 11th level is treated as invalid syntax. If a message gets near that, it has outgrown being one message; split it.

A `select` picks text by a value, such as a pronoun, and needs an `other` option:

```json
{ "replied": "{gender, select, female {She} male {He} other {They}} replied" }
```

To format a value in code, use the manager's formatters. They follow the active locale:

```ts
i18n.formatNumber(9.99, { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }); // "€9.99"
i18n.formatDate(new Date(), { dateStyle: "long" }); // "November 2, 2026"
i18n.formatRelativeTime(-1, "day", { numeric: "auto" }); // "yesterday"
i18n.formatList(["Ana", "Bia", "Caio"]); // "Ana, Bia, and Caio"
```

They take the same options as `Intl.NumberFormat`, `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat`, and `Intl.ListFormat`, read the same way `Intl` reads them, including options an object inherits, such as from a shared defaults object passed to `Object.create()`. They throw what those throw for invalid options.

### Time zones

Dates and times are written in the runtime's time zone. In a browser that is the reader's, which is usually right. On a server it is the server's, so 01:00 UTC on 2 November renders as "November 2" for a reader in São Paulo, where it is still 1 November, and the text changes once the browser takes over. Time zones: the reason a date is never just a date. Set `timeZone` to the zone the text should use:

```ts
createI18n({
  // ...
  timeZone: "America/Sao_Paulo",
});
```

It applies to `{d, date}`, `{d, time}`, and a date in `{d}`, and is `formatDate`'s default; `formatDate(value, { timeZone: "UTC" })` still overrides it. A zone `Intl` doesn't know throws a `TypeError` when the manager is created. On a server, set it per request, as in [Show dates in the reader's time zone](docs/server-rendering.md#show-dates-in-the-readers-time-zone).

### Literal braces and apostrophes

An apostrophe before `{` or `}` quotes text up to the next apostrophe, and two apostrophes make one. An apostrophe anywhere else is an ordinary apostrophe, so "Don't" needs nothing:

| Written in the dictionary | Shown                   |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `Don't forget {name}`     | `Don't forget Ana`      |
| `Type '{name}' to insert` | `Type {name} to insert` |
| `It''s '{'here'}'`        | `It's {here}`           |
| `Ouvrir l''{app}`         | `Ouvrir l'éditeur`      |
| `Ouvrir l’{app}`          | `Ouvrir l’éditeur`      |

Watch for an apostrophe right before a placeholder, as French, Italian, and Catalan elision puts one: `Ouvrir l'{app}` quotes `{app}`, so it shows `Ouvrir l{app}`, and nothing warns, because the text is valid. Write two apostrophes, `l''{app}`, or the typographic apostrophe `’`, which French typography prefers anyway and which is never syntax.

Inside a plural's forms, `#` stands for the number; write `'#'` for a literal `#`. A `select` nested in a form is not the plural itself, so a `#` there is shown as written, as in ICU; put `{count}` there instead. Quoted text is text to the types too: in `'{it''s {x}'`, which shows `{it's {x}`, `x` is not a value `t()` asks for.

Text that is not valid syntax, such as an unclosed `{` or a stray `}`, logs a warning, unless the manager is silent, and is shown with only its `{name}` placeholders filled. The warning names the key and the locale, and comes once for each text in each locale, among the 1,000 most recent. [Find untranslated keys](#find-untranslated-keys) shows a test that checks every message.

## Plurals

"1 items" is wrong in English, and other languages have more forms than English does. Arabic has six. To let each language choose, write the key as a group of forms instead of a single string:

```json
{
  "cart": {
    "items": {
      "one": "{count} item",
      "other": "{count} items"
    }
  }
}
```

Then pass a number as `count`:

```ts
t("cart.items", { count: 1 }); // "1 item"
t("cart.items", { count: 5 }); // "5 items"
```

The manager asks the built-in `Intl.PluralRules` which form the language uses for that number, and `count` also fills the `{count}` placeholder. The form names are the standard [CLDR plural categories](https://cldr.unicode.org/index/cldr-spec/plural-rules):

| Form    | Used for                                                                                       |
| ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `zero`  | Languages with a zero form, such as Arabic and Latvian. English uses `other` for 0.            |
| `one`   | Singular. French and Brazilian Portuguese (`pt`, `pt-BR`) also use it for 0; `pt-PT` does not. |
| `two`   | Dual, such as Arabic, Hebrew, and Welsh.                                                       |
| `few`   | Small numbers, such as 2–4 in Polish and Czech.                                                |
| `many`  | Large numbers in some languages, such as Polish and Arabic.                                    |
| `other` | Everything else. **Always include it**; it is the fallback for any form you leave out.         |

Each dictionary only needs the forms its own language uses: the English file has `one` and `other`, and the Arabic file has all six. Look up a language's forms in the [CLDR plural rules chart](https://www.unicode.org/cldr/charts/latest/supplemental/language_plural_rules.html).

When a plural group is missing from the current locale, the default locale's group is used, with the default language's rules, since that text is in the default language.

Three things to watch for:

- **`count` must be a number.** A string such as `"5"` does not select a form; the group is then treated as a missing key. Convert it where it comes in, such as `Number(params.get("count"))`. The manager doesn't guess, since `"1,5"` is one and a half in Portuguese and not a number at all to JavaScript.
- **A plain string under the same key wins over forms.** If `cart.items` is a string, `count` only fills `{count}`.
- **Without `other`, it is not a plural group.** `{ "one": "…", "two": "…" }` works only for counts whose form happens to be there; any other count shows the key. `has()` says such a group is not a key, and typed keys don't offer it. Add `other`.

### Show a formatted count

A plain `{count}` writes the number as JavaScript does, so 1234 items reads "1234 items" rather than "1,234 items", or "1.234 itens" in Portuguese. Write `{count, number}` in the forms instead:

```json
{
  "cart": {
    "items": {
      "one": "{count, number} item",
      "other": "{count, number} items"
    }
  }
}
```

```ts
t("cart.items", { count: 1234 }); // "1,234 items"
```

### Plurals inside a sentence

A plural group chooses the whole text. To choose only part of a sentence, or to give `0` its own wording, write an ICU plural in a single string. `#` is the number, formatted for the language, and `=N` matches an exact number before the forms are asked:

```json
{
  "inbox": "Hi {name}, {count, plural, =0 {you have no messages} one {you have # message} other {you have # messages}}."
}
```

```ts
t("inbox", { name: "Ana", count: 0 }); // "Hi Ana, you have no messages."
t("inbox", { name: "Ana", count: 1200 }); // "Hi Ana, you have 1,200 messages."
```

`=N` compares numbers, not text, so `=1`, `=1.0`, and `=01` all match 1. That also makes two of them in one message the same option twice: `{n, plural, =1 {…} =1.0 {…} other {…}}` is invalid syntax. Write each number once.

`offset:N` subtracts from the number before choosing a form and filling `#`, but not before matching `=N`, as in `{count, plural, offset:1 =0 {Nobody} =1 {{name}} one {{name} and # other} other {{name} and # others}}`, where a `count` of 2 shows `Ana and 1 other`. Both ways of writing plurals are supported; plural groups keep each form an ordinary key, which some translation tools handle better.

## Typed keys

When TypeScript can see your dictionary's type, `t()` only accepts keys that exist:

```ts
t("cart.items", { count: 2 }); // ok: a plural group
t("cart.items.one"); // ok: a single form is a key too
t("cart"); // compile error: a group of text is not a key
t("cart.itmes", { count: 2 }); // compile error: misspelled
```

The type comes from what your loader returns. If it returns several `as const` dictionaries, a key from any of them is accepted. If it returns `any` or `unknown`, as `response.json()` and dynamic imports do, every string is accepted; give the loader a return type, as in the JSON example above, to get checking back.

A key you build at runtime, such as ``t(`errors.${code}`)``, fails to compile even when it exists, because TypeScript can't know the value of `code`. Check it with `has()`, which narrows it to a key `t()` accepts, and pick a fallback when it isn't there:

```ts
const key = `errors.${code}`;
const message = i18n.has(key) ? i18n.t(key) : i18n.t("errors.unknown");
```

`has()` looks through the same dictionaries `t()` does. A plural group counts as a key when it has an `other` form, whatever language is active. A miss neither calls `onMissingKey` nor warns, since a key you expect to be missing sometimes is not a gap in the translations. A string no dictionary can hold, such as one with a line break or longer than 1,000 characters, is a miss too, so `code` can come from a response or a query string.

When you know the keys are there, cast it instead:

```ts
import type { TranslationKey } from "@codenhub/i18n";
import type en from "./locales/en.json";

type Key = TranslationKey<typeof en>;

t(`errors.${code}` as Key);
```

`TranslationKey` is also useful for typing a component prop or helper that takes a key.

### Typed values

When the default dictionary is an `as const` object in a `.ts` file, TypeScript sees each message's text, and `t()` also checks its values:

```ts
// locales/en.ts
export default {
  welcome: "Welcome back, {name}.",
  total: "Total: {amount, number}",
  cart: { items: { one: "{count} item", other: "{count} items" } },
} as const;
```

```ts
t("welcome", { name: "Ana" }); // ok
t("welcome"); // compile error: name is required
t("total", { amount: "3" }); // compile error: {amount, number} needs a number
t("cart.items", { count: 2 }); // ok: a plural group requires a numeric count
```

`number`, `plural`, and `selectordinal` arguments take a number, `date` and `time` take a `Date` or a timestamp, `select` takes a string or number, and a plain `{name}` takes any of these. Extra values are allowed. When several dictionaries are typed, a key needs the values of every one that has it.

A JSON import types every text as `string`, since TypeScript doesn't keep JSON string values, so a JSON dictionary checks keys but accepts any values. To check values, write the default language as `as const` TypeScript and keep the other languages in JSON, typed as the default:

```ts
import en from "./locales/en";

const loadLocale = async (locale: Locale): Promise<typeof en> => (locale === "en" ? en : (await import(`./locales/${locale}.json`)).default);
```

The loader's return type is what types `t()`, so a translation must use the same arguments as the default text; the compiler can't check the JSON files.

### When values aren't checked

Reading a message's arguments happens entirely in the type system, which is clever right up until it can't see the message. In these cases `t()` accepts any values, or none, for that key. Nothing fails to compile; the check is just off:

- **The key is one of several.** In `t(isError ? "save.failed" : "save.done")`, TypeScript sees a union of two keys and can't know which message's values apply. Call `t()` with each key in its own branch, `isError ? t("save.failed", { file }) : t("save.done")`, and each call is checked.
- **The message is a plain `string`**, as every text in a JSON dictionary is. Write the default language as `as const` TypeScript, as above.
- **The message has an unclosed `{`**, or a placeholder name that isn't ASCII letters, digits, and `_`, such as `{first-name}`. Other invalid syntax, such as `{n, number, currency}` or a `select` without `other`, may still ask for values. Either way, the runtime can't read it either: it logs a warning and shows the text with only valid `{name}` placeholders filled. Fix the message; the [message check](#find-untranslated-keys) finds these.
- **The message is too long for the types to read**: about 900 apostrophes, 450 arguments, or 900 spaces inside one argument's braces, in one text. TypeScript has a limit on how deep a type can go, and the reading stops short of it instead of failing your build. At runtime the message works normally. If you have one of these, it is probably three messages in a trench coat; splitting it brings the checks back.
- **The manager's type is written by hand without the dictionary.** `I18n<"en" | "pt", Key>` checks keys but not values. Pass the dictionary type as a third type argument, `I18n<"en" | "pt", Key, typeof en>`, to keep them checked.

### Write the types yourself

If you write the manager's type yourself, as in `let i18n: I18n<"en" | "pt">`, pass the key type too: `I18n<"en" | "pt", Key>`. The second type argument defaults to `string`, which accepts any key. `createI18n()` fills it in for you.

Let TypeScript infer the manager's types from the configuration. Passing some type arguments yourself, such as `createI18n<"en" | "pt">(...)`, turns off inference for the rest, and keys go back to plain `string`.

If you keep the configuration in a separate variable, mark the default locale `as const`:

```ts
const config = {
  locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en" as const,
  loadLocale: (locale: "en" | "pt") => dictionaries[locale],
};
```

Without `as const`, TypeScript sees `defaultLocale` as any `string`, and `createI18n(config)` reports that `string` is not `"en" | "pt"`.

## Find untranslated keys

A key missing from one language quietly shows default-language text, which is easy to miss. Catch it in a test by comparing every dictionary with the default one. `loadLocale()` returns a dictionary without changing the manager's language:

```ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { i18n } from "./i18n";

// Plural forms other than `other` differ by language, so they are not compared.
// A key such as `settings.one` is still compared unless its group also has `other`.
const isLanguageSpecificForm = (key: string, dictionary: Readonly<Record<string, string>>) => {
  const form = /^(.+)\.(zero|one|two|few|many)$/.exec(key);
  return form !== null && `${form[1]}.other` in dictionary;
};

test("every locale has every key", async () => {
  const defaults = await i18n.loadLocale(i18n.defaultLocale);
  const reference = Object.keys(defaults).filter((key) => !isLanguageSpecificForm(key, defaults));

  for (const locale of i18n.locales) {
    const dictionary = await i18n.loadLocale(locale);
    const missing = reference.filter((key) => !(key in dictionary));
    expect(missing, `missing in ${locale}`).toEqual([]);
  }
});
```

To catch a message with broken syntax, such as an unclosed `{` a translator left, look up every key in every locale and fail on the warning. The manager must not be silent for this:

```ts
import { expect, test, vi } from "vitest";
import { i18n } from "./i18n";

test("every message is valid", async () => {
  const warn = vi.spyOn(console, "warn").mockImplementation(() => {});
  await i18n.init();

  for (const locale of i18n.locales) {
    await i18n.setLocale(locale);
    for (const key of Object.keys(await i18n.loadLocale(locale))) {
      i18n.t(key as Parameters<typeof i18n.t>[0]);
    }
  }

  expect(warn.mock.calls.filter(([text]) => String(text).startsWith("[I18n] Invalid message"))).toEqual([]);
  warn.mockRestore();
});
```

To fail a test on keys missing from every dictionary, such as a typo in a key you built at runtime, throw from `onMissingKey`:

```ts
createI18n({
  // ...
  onMissingKey(key, locale) {
    throw new Error(`Missing translation "${key}" in ${locale}`);
  },
});
```

## Size limits

Dictionaries come from files and servers, and now and then a file or server sends something that isn't a dictionary at all: a truncated download, a misconfigured proxy, or something built on purpose to be huge. So the manager caps how large one can be, which stops a corrupted or hostile file from freezing the page. The defaults fit any real app:

| Limit                      | Default   | Option            |
| -------------------------- | --------- | ----------------- |
| Nesting depth              | 100       | `maxDepth`        |
| Translations               | 10,000    | `maxTranslations` |
| Keys and groups together   | 20,000    | `maxProperties`   |
| Characters in one text     | 100,000   | `maxValueLength`  |
| Characters in all texts    | 5,000,000 | `maxTotalLength`  |
| Characters in one full key | 1,000     | fixed             |

Raise one with `dictionaryLimits`, which keeps the default for any limit you leave out:

```ts
createI18n({
  // ...
  dictionaryLimits: { maxTranslations: 50_000, maxProperties: 100_000 },
});
```

Each limit must be a positive whole number, and a name that isn't one of the five throws a `TypeError` when the manager is created. A nested dictionary counts each group as a property, so raising `maxTranslations` often means raising `maxProperties` too. Raising `maxDepth` past 499 does nothing: each level adds at least a letter and a dot to the full key, so a text that deep would break the fixed 1,000-character key limit first.

## Next

With your dictionaries written, put them in front of someone. In a browser, continue with [Translate a browser app](docs/browser.md). On a server or in a static build, skip to [Render on a server or at build time](docs/server-rendering.md).

<!-- Source: docs/browser.md -->

# Translate a browser app

In a browser, the manager from the [overview](docs/index.md) still does the translating. `@codenhub/i18n/browser` adds the parts only a browser has: the visitor's language settings, a place to remember their choice, and the page itself. This page sets those up for the `en` and `pt` app from the overview.

## Start with `initializeBrowserI18n`

Use `initializeBrowserI18n()` instead of `i18n.init()`. It picks a locale, starts the manager with it, and then keeps the page in step:

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { initializeBrowserI18n } from "@codenhub/i18n/browser";
import { i18n } from "./i18n";

await initializeBrowserI18n({ i18n });
```

With no other options, this:

1. Picks the visitor's locale (see below) and loads it.
2. Sets `<html lang="pt" dir="ltr">` to match, so screen readers pronounce text correctly and [right-to-left languages](docs/index.md#right-to-left-languages) lay out correctly.
3. Saves the language your app chooses, and reads it back on the visitor's next visit.

It returns a binding with a `disconnect()` method; you only need it when you tear the app down, as in tests or micro-frontends.

### How the locale is chosen

The first of these that gives a supported locale wins:

1. The `locale` option, when you pass one. It counts as your app's choice, so it is also saved, unless `persistLocale` is `false`.
2. The visitor's saved choice from an earlier visit.
3. The browser's language settings, `navigator.languages`, matched to your locales with [`matchLocale()`](docs/index.md#turn-outside-input-into-a-locale). A visitor whose browser asks for `pt-BR` gets your `pt`.
4. Your default locale.

Pass `locale` when the page already knows its language, such as from the URL in [a localized site](docs/localized-urls.md#read-the-locale-on-the-client). It then overrides everything else, so the browser can't disagree with the server about which language the page is in.

On a localized site, that means every page view saves the language in its URL. Usually that is what you want: the saved language is the one the visitor last read, which is what [the static-site redirect](docs/localized-urls.md#detect-the-language-on-a-static-site) relies on. It also means a visitor who follows one shared Portuguese link has Portuguese saved from then on, until they read a page in another language, even if their browser asks for English. If you would rather save only what the visitor picks in your language picker, turn saving off with `persistLocale: false` and store the picker's choice yourself. That option also stops the binding from reading the saved choice, so read your own back and pass it as `locale`.

If your loader fails for a saved locale, the binding warns and tries the locale it detects from the browser, then the default locale, so the visitor still gets a language they read instead of a broken app. A detected locale that fails falls back to the default the same way. The saved choice is kept for next time. A loader failure for a locale you passed explicitly, or for the default locale, still rejects, since there is nothing sensible to fall back to. So does a dictionary that loads but [breaks the rules](docs/troubleshooting.md#a-dictionary-is-rejected), whatever the locale: that is a bug to fix, not a network hiccup to ride out.

## Let visitors switch languages

Call `setLocale()` from your language picker. The binding reacts to every change that is applied: it saves the choice and updates `lang` and `dir`.

```ts
const picker = document.querySelector<HTMLSelectElement>("#language")!;

picker.value = i18n.locale;
picker.addEventListener("change", async () => {
  await i18n.setLocale(picker.value as (typeof i18n.locales)[number]);
});
```

A visitor who changes their mind quickly is handled for you: when two switches overlap, the later one wins, and the earlier one resolves without changing anything, as [The latest call wins](docs/index.md#the-latest-call-wins) explains. So read `i18n.locale` after the `await` rather than assuming the picker's value.

Only choices your app makes are saved: the `locale` option, and every applied `setLocale()` or `init()` after the binding has started. A language detected from the browser settings is not, and neither is the default locale the binding fell back to. A visitor who never picked one keeps following their browser settings, including when you add their language later.

The choice is stored in `localStorage` as `{"locale":"pt"}` under the key `"i18n"`. Change the key with `storageKey`, or turn saving off with `persistLocale: false`. If storage is unavailable, as in some private browsing modes, the binding warns and carries on without it.

## Re-render a framework

Frameworks such as React, Vue, Svelte, or Solid render the text themselves by calling `t()`. They need to know when to render again, and `i18n.subscribe()` tells them: it calls your function after every applied `init()` and every applied language change, and returns a function that stops it. A `setLocale()` to the language already showing, or one overtaken by a later call, changes nothing and calls nothing.

In React, `useSyncExternalStore` connects the two:

```tsx
import { useSyncExternalStore } from "react";
import { i18n, t } from "./i18n";

export function useLocale() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(i18n.subscribe, () => i18n.locale);
}

export function CartBadge({ count }: { count: number }) {
  useLocale(); // re-renders this component when the language changes
  return <span>{t("cart.items", { count })}</span>;
}
```

Other frameworks follow the same pattern: store `i18n.locale` in a reactive value and update it from `subscribe()`.

## Translate HTML without a framework

For static pages, or HTML your framework doesn't render, the binding can translate the page itself. Mark elements with the key, and pass the part of the page to translate as `root`:

```html
<h1 data-i18n="home.title">Welcome</h1>
<input data-i18n-placeholder="search.hint" placeholder="Search" />
<button data-i18n-aria-label="menu.open"><svg>…</svg></button>
```

```ts
await initializeBrowserI18n({ i18n, root: document });
```

- `data-i18n` replaces an element's text. The element must contain only text, with no child elements, so a translation can never remove your markup. Elements with children are skipped with a warning.
- `data-i18n-<attribute>` translates one attribute. Only attributes that hold text for people or screen readers are allowed: `alt`, `title`, `placeholder`, `label`, `aria-label`, `aria-description`, `aria-placeholder`, `aria-roledescription`, and `aria-valuetext`. Others, such as `data-i18n-href` or `data-i18n-onclick`, are ignored, so a translation can never change a link, a style, or an event handler.
- The text already in the HTML is the last fallback. A key a language lacks shows the text of the next locale in its fallback chain, as `t()` does: a configured parent such as `pt` for `pt-BR`, then the default locale. The original text comes back only when no dictionary in the chain has the key.
- Text is set as plain text, never as HTML, and `<script>`, `<style>`, `<noscript>`, and `<template>` are never touched.
- Placeholders such as `{name}` are not filled here, because there is nowhere in the HTML to pass a value from. Render text with values from your code with `t()`.
- The page shows the text written in its HTML until the visitor's dictionary has loaded, then switches in place, which on a slow connection is visible. To avoid that, render a page per language ahead of time, as in [Build a static site](docs/server-rendering.md#build-a-static-site), and pass its `locale`; or keep the root hidden until the binding's promise settles.

### Form controls

Two form elements need care, because their text is also what the form sends:

- **Give every translated `<option>` a `value`.** An option without one submits its text, so `<option data-i18n="plan.basic">Basic</option>` submits `Básico` once the page is in Portuguese, and your server receives a word it has never heard of. Write `<option value="basic" data-i18n="plan.basic">Basic</option>`, and the form sends `basic` in every language.
- **Use `<button>` for a translated submit button.** The label of `<input type="submit" value="Send">` is its `value`, and `value` is not an attribute the binding translates, since it is also data the form sends. `<button type="submit" data-i18n="form.send">Send</button>` translates like any other text.

### Watch for changes

The page is retranslated on every language change. To also translate elements your code adds later, turn on `observe`:

```ts
await initializeBrowserI18n({ i18n, root: document.querySelector("#app")!, observe: true });
```

With `observe`, adding an element, or changing or removing a `data-i18n` key, is handled as it happens. That includes elements other code adds while the binding is translating, such as a custom element that renders children when its attribute changes. The binding handles those once per pass: if that code changes a key again in response, as an element that keeps resetting its own `data-i18n-*` attribute would, the second change waits for the next locale change instead of starting an endless loop. An element that is added and then moved out of `root` before the binding gets to it is not translated: by then it belongs to another part of the page.

Leave `observe` off when a framework renders the page: the framework already calls `t()`, and watching the page would only duplicate its work.

The binding does not look inside custom elements (tags with a dash, such as `<my-widget>`), with or without a shadow root, and doesn't warn when it skips one. A component has a life of its own: it can render after the page was translated, and it adds and removes text as people use it, which it has to translate itself anyway. So the component translates its own content: call `i18n.t()` when it renders, and render again from `i18n.subscribe()`:

```ts
class ProductCard extends HTMLElement {
  #unsubscribe?: () => void;

  connectedCallback() {
    // The element can connect before the manager is ready; `subscribe()` also calls back once `init()` applies.
    this.#unsubscribe = i18n.subscribe(() => this.render());
    if (i18n.isReady) {
      this.render();
    }
  }

  disconnectedCallback() {
    this.#unsubscribe?.();
  }

  render() {
    this.querySelector("button")!.textContent = i18n.t("cart.add");
  }
}
```

That includes a custom element used only as a wrapper, whose children you wrote in the page, such as `<site-nav><a data-i18n="nav.home">Home</a></site-nav>`: those links are skipped too. Use a plain element, such as `<nav>`, for a wrapper whose text the page translates. A component can't have a binding of its own on the same manager, since a manager has one binding.

## In a Web Worker

A Web Worker has no page, so there is no `<html>` to set `lang` on and nothing to translate. The core manager and `@codenhub/i18n/routing` work there as they do anywhere. The browser binding can still pick and save the locale, if you turn off the parts that need a page:

```ts
// worker.ts
await initializeBrowserI18n({ i18n, syncDocument: false });
```

Pass `syncDocument: false` and no `root`. With the default `syncDocument: true` and no `document`, `initializeBrowserI18n()` throws `TypeError: [I18n] Document synchronization requires a page document; pass syncDocument: false without one.` before it starts the manager, so the manager is left not started rather than half bound. A worker has no `localStorage` either, so saving warns and is skipped; add `persistLocale: false` to start quietly.

## Options

| Option          | Default    | What it does                                                                                                 |
| --------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `i18n`          | (required) | The manager to start.                                                                                        |
| `locale`        | none       | A locale that overrides saved and detected ones. It is saved too while `persistLocale` is on.                |
| `persistLocale` | `true`     | Read the saved choice, and save the `locale` option and every language change your app makes after start.    |
| `storageKey`    | `"i18n"`   | The `localStorage` key for the saved choice.                                                                 |
| `syncDocument`  | `true`     | Keep `<html lang>` and `dir` in step with the locale. Needs a page `document`; pass `false` in a Web Worker. |
| `root`          | none       | The part of the page to translate with `data-i18n` attributes.                                               |
| `observe`       | `false`    | Also translate changes below `root` as they happen. Needs `root`.                                            |

## Rules to know

- **One binding per manager.** A second `initializeBrowserI18n()` call for the same manager rejects until the first is disconnected.
- **Let the binding start the manager.** If your code calls `i18n.init()` before the binding's locale is active, or calls `i18n.setLocale()` then on a manager that was already initialized, even to the locale already showing, the binding's promise rejects with `Error: [I18n] Browser initialization was superseded before its locale became active.`. The manager keeps the later call's result, under [the latest-call rule](docs/index.md#the-latest-call-wins), and the binding is not connected. On a manager that was not initialized yet, `setLocale()` just fails with its own error and the binding carries on. Calling `init()` or `setLocale()` after the binding's promise has resolved is fine.
- **`disconnect()` stops reacting but undoes nothing.** It stops saving, syncing, and translating, but leaves the current text, attributes, and saved choice as they are. You can then start a new binding.

The [browser reference](docs/reference/browser.md) documents every option and failure, and [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md#the-browser-binding-warns-or-rejects) lists each warning the binding logs.

## Next

A browser app that is also rendered on a server, or built ahead of time, has a second half: [Render on a server or at build time](docs/server-rendering.md) covers it, including how to hand the server's locale to the browser. If your app only ever runs in the browser and puts the language in its URLs, go straight to [Localized URLs](docs/localized-urls.md).

<!-- Source: docs/server-rendering.md -->

# Render on a server or at build time

A browser has one visitor, so one manager is right. A server has many visitors at once, in different languages, and a manager speaks one language at a time. So: **one manager per page you render**. A static site build renders every language in one run and follows the same rule. This page shows that shape with the `en` and `pt` dictionaries from the [overview](docs/index.md#walkthrough), then picks each visitor's language, gets their dates right, and keeps the logs readable.

## One manager per request

A manager has one current language. If two requests shared one, a Portuguese request calling `setLocale("pt")` would change the language of an English page still rendering, and the English visitor would get a page that switches language halfway down. It works fine in development, where you are the only visitor. So create the manager inside the request:

```ts
// src/i18n.ts
import { createI18n } from "@codenhub/i18n";
import { dictionaries } from "./locales";

export const createAppI18n = () =>
  createI18n({
    locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
    defaultLocale: "en",
    loadLocale: (locale) => dictionaries[locale],
  });
```

```ts
// src/render.ts
import { createAppI18n } from "./i18n";

export async function renderPage(request: Request) {
  const i18n = createAppI18n();
  await i18n.init({ locale: pickLocale(i18n, request) });
  const { t } = i18n;

  return `<!doctype html>
<html lang="${i18n.locale}" dir="${i18n.direction}">
  <title>${escapeHtml(t("home.title"))}</title>
</html>`;
}
```

Creating a manager is cheap, and the work that isn't is shared. When your loader returns the same object on every call, as an imported module does, every manager reuses the one checked copy of that dictionary instead of checking it again. A loader that reads and parses a file on every call loses that, so read each file once and keep the result.

`i18n.direction` is `"rtl"` for a right-to-left locale such as Arabic, and `"ltr"` otherwise; [Right-to-left languages](docs/index.md#right-to-left-languages) explains how it is decided and how to override it. Put it in `<html dir>`, as above, and the browser lays the page out the right way round from the first byte.

Pass the manager, or `t`, down to whatever renders the page, rather than importing a shared one.

`t()` returns plain text. Escape it before putting it into HTML, as you would any other text, or let your template engine do it.

## Choose a locale from `Accept-Language`

Browsers send the visitor's languages in the `Accept-Language` header, such as `pt-BR,pt;q=0.9,en;q=0.8`. Turn it into a list, most preferred first, and let `matchLocale()` pick the best locale you support:

```ts
import type { I18n } from "@codenhub/i18n";

// Real browsers send a handful of languages, and a header can list thousands.
const MAX_PREFERENCES = 10;

function pickLocale<TLocale extends string>(i18n: I18n<TLocale>, request: Request): TLocale {
  const preferences = (request.headers.get("accept-language") ?? "")
    .split(",")
    .map((entry) => {
      const [tag = "", ...parameters] = entry.split(";");
      const weight = parameters.map((parameter) => parameter.trim()).find((parameter) => /^q=/i.test(parameter));
      // A weight is 0 to 1 with up to three decimals; anything else, such as `q=0x1`, is malformed.
      const quality = weight === undefined ? 1 : /^q=(0(\.\d{0,3})?|1(\.0{0,3})?)$/i.test(weight) ? Number(weight.slice(2)) : 0;
      return { tag: tag.trim(), quality };
    })
    // Drops refused languages (q=0) and malformed weights.
    .filter(({ quality }) => quality > 0)
    .sort((left, right) => right.quality - left.quality)
    .slice(0, MAX_PREFERENCES)
    .map(({ tag }) => tag);

  return i18n.matchLocale(preferences) ?? i18n.defaultLocale;
}
```

A visitor whose languages all fail to match, including one who refuses your default with `en;q=0`, still gets the default locale, since the page has to be in some language. This helper does not implement the rest of `Accept-Language`, such as `*`; use your server framework's parser if you need it, and pass its result to `matchLocale()`.

`matchLocale()` takes a list rather than the header because parsing the header, and limiting its size, belongs to your server. Keep the limit: `matchLocale()` tries preferences in order until one matches, so a request whose 16 KB header lists thousands of languages you don't support would otherwise hold your server's event loop for tens of milliseconds, about 60 ms on Node 24. It matches the same way the browser binding does, so a visitor gets the same language from the server as from the browser: `pt-BR` gets your `pt`, and `zh-TW` gets your `zh-Hant`. Malformed tags are skipped, and `undefined` means nothing matched. [Turn outside input into a locale](docs/index.md#turn-outside-input-into-a-locale) has the full matching order, including which of two regional locales wins, and `resolveLocale()` for a locale from a cookie or a query string.

When the URL carries the language, as on [a localized site](docs/localized-urls.md), read it from the URL instead and use `Accept-Language` only to choose where to redirect a visitor who arrives at `/`. A static site has no server to see the header; see [Detect the language on a static site](docs/localized-urls.md#detect-the-language-on-a-static-site).

## Show dates in the reader's time zone

A server formats dates in its own time zone, which is rarely the reader's. Text such as "Shipped on {date, date, long}" can then show another day than the reader's calendar, and change when the browser takes over. Give each request's manager the reader's zone, such as one your app stores per account or the browser reports in a cookie:

```ts
export const createAppI18n = (timeZone?: string) =>
  createI18n({
    locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
    defaultLocale: "en",
    loadLocale: (locale) => dictionaries[locale],
    timeZone,
  });
```

`Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone` reads the zone in the browser. A zone `Intl` doesn't know throws a `TypeError`, so check a value from a cookie before using it, or fall back to a fixed zone such as `"UTC"`.

## Keep production logs useful

A missing key logs a warning once for each locale and key in each manager. With a manager per request, that is once per request, so one missing key on the home page becomes a log line for every visitor. In production, send misses to your logger, where you can count them instead of scrolling past them, or turn the warnings off:

```ts
createI18n({
  // ...
  onMissingKey(key, locale) {
    logger.warn({ key, locale }, "missing translation");
  },
});
```

`onMissingKey` replaces the warning and runs on every miss. `isSilent: true` turns off warnings only, including the one for a message with invalid syntax. Errors, such as a failed load, still throw.

In Node.js, an exception thrown from a function passed to `subscribe()`, or from a `ready` or `locale-change` listener, crashes the process, as with any `EventTarget`. Servers rarely need these, but if you use them, wrap their body in `try`/`catch` so they can't throw.

## Build a static site

A static build renders every page in every language ahead of time. It follows the same rule: one manager per page. List your localized pages with [locale routing](docs/localized-urls.md#generate-every-localized-page), then render each one:

```ts
import { createLocaleRouting } from "@codenhub/i18n/routing";
import { createAppI18n } from "./i18n";

const routing = createLocaleRouting({
  locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  localePrefix: "except-default",
});

// Your pages, keyed by their canonical path: the path without a locale, in the words your code routes on.
const pages = { "/": renderHome, "/about": renderAbout };

const builds = Object.entries(pages).flatMap(([page, render]) => routing.localizeAll(page).map(({ locale, pathname }) => ({ locale, pathname, render })));
// [{ locale: "en", pathname: "/", render: renderHome }, { locale: "pt", pathname: "/pt", render: renderHome }, ...]

await Promise.all(
  builds.map(async ({ locale, pathname, render }) => {
    const i18n = createAppI18n();
    await i18n.init({ locale });
    await writePage(pathname, render(i18n.t));
  }),
);
```

`pathname` is a URL path, percent-encoded where the table has words such as `/serviços`. Hosts decode a request before looking for its file, so name the file after `decodeURI(pathname)`: `serviços` for `/servi%C3%A7os`, not the encoded form, which no request finds. Where that file goes, such as `serviços.html` or `serviços/index.html`, depends on your host and your `trailingSlash` setting.

A dictionary that fails to load or check makes `init()` reject, so the build fails instead of publishing pages without text. A key that only your default language has does not fail the build; it renders in the default language. Add [the untranslated-keys test](docs/translations.md#find-untranslated-keys) to catch those, and make `onMissingKey` throw during the build to fail on keys missing from every language.

## Hand the locale to the browser

When the browser takes over a server-rendered page, it must start in the language the server used, or the text changes as the page loads. Pass that locale explicitly; it overrides saved and detected ones, and the binding saves it as the visitor's choice, as [How the locale is chosen](docs/browser.md#how-the-locale-is-chosen) explains:

```ts
await initializeBrowserI18n({ i18n, locale: document.documentElement.lang as "en" | "pt" });
```

On a localized site, read it from the URL with `routing.parse()` instead, as [Localized URLs](docs/localized-urls.md#read-the-locale-on-the-client) shows.

## Next

If the language of each page lives in its URL, as it does on most server-rendered and static sites, continue with [Localized URLs](docs/localized-urls.md): it reads the locale from the path, builds links to other languages, and lists every page a static build needs.

<!-- Source: docs/localized-urls.md -->

# Localized URLs

Giving each language its own URL, such as `/about` and `/pt/about`, lets people share a link in the language they read, and lets search engines index every language. `@codenhub/i18n/routing` handles the part that is the same in every framework: reading the locale from a path, and building the path for another locale. It can also translate the path itself, so the Portuguese about page is `/pt/sobre`, or even just `/sobre`. The examples continue the `en` and `pt` app from the earlier pages, with Spanish joining once paths get translated.

## Set up routing

```ts
// src/routing.ts
import { createLocaleRouting } from "@codenhub/i18n/routing";

export const routing = createLocaleRouting({
  locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  localePrefix: "except-default",
});
```

`localePrefix` decides which paths start with their locale. It is required and has no default, because each choice gives your site different URLs, and URLs are hard to change once people have bookmarked them. Leaving it out throws `TypeError: [I18n] Invalid locale routing configuration: localePrefix: Expected "always", "except-default", or "when-ambiguous", received undefined`.

| `localePrefix`     | English about page | Portuguese about page                                                             |
| ------------------ | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"except-default"` | `/about`           | `/pt/about`                                                                       |
| `"always"`         | `/en/about`        | `/pt/about`                                                                       |
| `"when-ambiguous"` | `/about`           | `/pt/about`, or `/sobre` once translated; see [Drop the prefix](#drop-the-prefix) |

`"except-default"` keeps your existing URLs when you add a language. `"always"` makes every URL name its language, so `/about` is not a page, which suits a site that redirects `/` to the visitor's language. `"when-ambiguous"` drops the prefix from translated paths that can only belong to one language, and is worth reading about before you pick it.

Use the same `locales` and `defaultLocale` as your manager. Routing is separate from the manager, so it also works where no translation happens, such as in a server's redirect logic.

If you keep the configuration in a variable before passing it in, write `localePrefix: "except-default" as const`. Without `as const`, TypeScript widens the value to `string`, and `createLocaleRouting` rejects it at compile time.

### Trailing slashes

By default, `localize()` keeps the slash of the path you give it: `/about/` gives `/pt/about/`, and `/about` gives `/pt/about`. A locale's home page has no slash to keep, since `/` says nothing about one, so it is always `/pt`. Many static hosts serve `pt/index.html` at `/pt/` and redirect `/pt` there, so on a site like that, set `trailingSlash`:

```ts
export const routing = createLocaleRouting({
  locales: ["en", "pt"] as const,
  defaultLocale: "en",
  localePrefix: "except-default",
  trailingSlash: "always",
});

routing.localize("/", "pt"); // "/pt/"
routing.localize("/about", "pt"); // "/pt/about/"
routing.localize("/", "en"); // "/"
```

| `trailingSlash`          | Builds                                                         |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"preserve"`, by default | The given path's slash: `/pt/about/` or `/pt/about`, and `/pt` |
| `"always"`               | A slash on every path: `/pt/about/` and `/pt/`                 |
| `"never"`                | No slash on any path but `/`: `/pt/about` and `/pt`            |

`parse()` accepts both spellings whatever you choose, and its `pathname` keeps the request's slash: `/about` for `/pt/about` and `/about/` for `/pt/about/`. Route both values to the same page, or strip the slash before routing. With `"always"` or `"never"`, [Redirect to the canonical URL](#redirect-to-the-canonical-url) then sends the other spelling to the one `localize()` builds, so each page has one address.

## Read the locale from a path

`parse()` splits a path into its locale and the rest:

```ts
routing.parse("/pt/about"); // { locale: "pt", pathname: "/about" }
routing.parse("/about"); // { locale: "en", pathname: "/about" }
routing.parse("/PT/about"); // { locale: "pt", pathname: "/about" }
```

The `pathname` it returns is the **canonical path**: the path your application routes on, the same in every language. Hold on to that idea; it matters once paths are translated.

`parse()` returns `undefined` for a path that is not a page in any locale, such as `/pt/en/about`: once its prefix is removed it starts with another locale, so no link ever leads there. Answer it with a 404.

With `localePrefix: "always"`, a path without a locale returns `undefined` too, so you can redirect it. Add the chosen locale's prefix and parse that, so a path in that locale's words, such as `/sobre`, is read as one, and a path that is no page in that locale either gets its 404:

```ts
const route = routing.parse(url.pathname);
if (route === undefined) {
  const locale = pickLocale(i18n, request);
  const guess = routing.parse(`/${locale}${url.pathname === "/" ? "" : url.pathname}`);
  if (guess === undefined) {
    return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 });
  }
  const target = new URL(url);
  target.pathname = routing.localize(guess.pathname, guess.locale);
  return Response.redirect(target, 302);
}
```

`pickLocale` is the `Accept-Language` helper from [Render on a server](docs/server-rendering.md#choose-a-locale-from-accept-language).

### Read the locale on the client

In the browser, take the locale from the URL and pass it to the browser binding. The URL then wins over the visitor's saved and detected languages, so the page always matches its address:

```ts
import { initializeBrowserI18n } from "@codenhub/i18n/browser";
import { i18n } from "./i18n";
import { routing } from "./routing";

const route = routing.parse(window.location.pathname);
await initializeBrowserI18n({ i18n, locale: route?.locale });
```

### Redirect to the canonical URL

`parse()` is forgiving: `/PT/about` and `/en/about` are read as well as `/pt/about` and `/about`, and so are both spellings of a [trailing slash](#trailing-slashes). That is friendly to someone typing a URL, but a search engine that finds one page at several addresses splits its ranking between them. Send every other spelling to the one `localize()` builds. Every path `parse()` returns has one, so this never throws:

